✍️ Gaming Industry Trends & Market Insights

The World Does Not End When the Sequel Arrives: The Perpetuation of Live Services 🌐

Massive digital worlds built over more than a decade no longer shut their gates in front of next-generation sequels.
Why has the traditional success formula of 'generational transition via sequels' become obsolete in the live-service era?
Rockstar Games announced that it will continue supporting the existing 'GTA Online' even after the release of 'GTA 6.' 🎮 Blizzard is also seeking to perpetuate the classic experience through 'World of Warcraft: Forever.' These represent a symbolic moment signaling the complete collapse of the past console and PC packaged-game formula, where the launch of a sequel inevitably meant the demise of the preceding world.

This shift directly impacts modern gamers' consumption habits and psychology. 👥 For players who deeply resist having years of accumulated assets and social networks wiped out, preserving older titles serves as a vital psychological safety net. For developers, it prevents churn among players who struggle to adapt to the new game, while securing platform stability by operating simultaneous monetization pipelines across both older and newer generations within a single IP.

Today, major IPs function not merely as one-off software products, but as virtual platforms that form their own societies. 🏛️ Even when a technologically revolutionary sequel emerges, there is little reason to forcibly dismantle a thriving hub where a massive economy and community have already taken root. Ultimately, the crux of the future gaming industry lies not in 'forcing a one-sided migration to the next title,' but in how flexibly studios can design the 'parallel coexistence of generational experiences.'

Can the promising new world promised by cutting-edge technology truly create synergy with a familiar, time-tested old world? 🧭 Developers now face the test of executing sophisticated live operations capable of sustaining two massive worlds simultaneously amidst a divided player pool.
— Dr. K
